text: Welcome, curators. Our museum is building a diorama of a Haudenosaunee longhouse. Visit one in VR, then record a short video for me.
No headset today? Come to the collections room. Put each museum card on the timeline. Then tell me what you found.
Have more time? Turn slowly while you record, so I can see both ends of the longhouse.
Before your headset, look at how a longhouse is built. Then press Practice and say your two sentences before the timer ends.
Open the On-Demand app. Click Explore. Type Longhouse in the filter box, click Iroquois Longhouse, then click Begin Solo.
Move with the thumbstick. Look at the walls and the roof. Find one spot where you can see a lot of the longhouse.
Open Library, then Camera. Click Record video and say your two sentences. Click again to stop. Then send it on the Canvas tab.
Press the Meta button and click Quit. Then open the Canvas assignment and check that your video is there.

All four labels are up! Now look at the postcards. Each one is a real photo from our region. Turn each postcard over and read the back. It tells you where the photo was taken. Then pin it on that place on the map.

Last job of the day! Visitors need to know where they are, so you'll write the gallery introduction. First, finish the direction sentence. Tap a direction word for each blank. Then add one sentence of your own. When it's ready, open your gallery!
Finish the direction sentence. Then add one sentence of your own. Then open your gallery.
Look at the space picture first. Then drag the slider to the right to add the map lines.
Read the clue on the label. Then tap the place on the map where it belongs.

Hoo, hello, curator! You finished the World Map Hall. Now a brand-new room is ready: the North America and Caribbean Gallery. To get there, start with the big globe. Turn the globe. Zoom in. And remember our lens today, courtesy. Real people live in every place we study, so we say each name with care.

Welcome to the gallery! The big map on the wall shows one part of the world. Four places on it are waiting for labels. Read the clue on each label. Use the compass rose to find north, south, east, and west. Then tap the place where the label belongs.
Here's a puzzle for you. Canada and the United States are next-door neighbors. Which one is bigger? And which one has more people? Press the buttons one at a time and find out.
This is our region seen from space. NASA made this picture from lots of satellite photos. Look closely at the land first. Then use the slider to add the map lines, and watch what changes.

Here is the label cart. Every label is hidden under a cloth. Lift the cloth on one label. Look at the photo and read the clue. Then tap the drawer it belongs in: mountains, rivers, plains, or islands.

Last job of the day! Our physical map needs a label for visitors. Pick a photo for your label. Then write your label in the Curator Task box. Name a mountain range, a river, and one more feature, and say where each one is. When you're ready, open your exhibit!
Lift the cloth on one label. Look at the photo and read the clue. Then tap the drawer where it belongs.
Pick a photo. Write your label in the Curator Task box above. Then press Open my exhibit.
Do the steps one at a time: tilt the map, cut the slice, then walk across it.

Hoo, hello again, curator! Last time we hung the country labels on the big wall map. Today a cart full of brand-new labels has rolled into the museum. These labels are not for countries. They are for the land itself. And remember our lens, courtesy. Many of today's names, like Mississippi and Appalachian, come from the first peoples who lived here. So we say each name with care.
What happens when rain falls on tall mountains? Make it rain on the Rocky Mountains. Then follow the water and watch where every river goes.
This is a real physical map of our region. A physical map shows the land, not the countries. Use the color key to read it. Then turn on the borders and look closely at the mountains.
Welcome to the relief table! Right now it looks like a flat map. Tilt the map, and watch the land stand up. Then cut a slice across the United States, and walk across it from west to east.
Here's the Exhibit Floor! Visitors will read the label you write. A good label tells what the resource is, where it comes from, how people use it, and one honest limit. You've got this!

Welcome to the Gallery! Our biggest exhibit is the Time-Lapse Case. It is a model with four glass boxes: a forest, two fish tanks, and oil under the ground. First you'll make a guess. Then you'll watch people use the resources. Then you'll drag the time lever to the right to move forward in time. Let's see what happens!
Drag each specimen into the case where it belongs. Or tap a specimen, then tap a case.
Press and hold a crate until the lid pops off. Then do the steps on the desk, one at a time.
Pick one specimen. Then write your label in the Curator Task box. Your words show up under your specimen as you type. When you have twenty words, tap Open my exhibit.

Hoo, hello, curator! Big news. Six crates just came in the back door of our North America and Caribbean Gallery. Inside are things the land gives us, like wood, wheat, water, fish, copper, and oil. Each crate has a tag that says where it came from. But a tag doesn't tell the whole story. Your job today is to find out how people use each one. And be honest about something curators sometimes leave out: not everything the land gives us lasts forever.
All six are in the log! Did you notice? Bread, paper, fish sticks, and gas did not start at a store. They all started on the land. Next, walk through the door to the Gallery. That's room two.
Time to fill the display cases! Every object from the crates goes in one of two cases. Think back to the time lever. Which ones came back?

These are real photos taken long ago, in three different places on the Great Plains. The Great Plains are the wide, flat lands in the middle of our country. Tap each small photo to see it big. Then tap the numbered dots to learn what you're looking at.

Here's a little experiment. Two trays hold the same soil. Tray 1 has bare soil. Tray 2 has grass growing in it. A fan will blow the same wind on both. First, make a guess. Which tray will keep more of its soil?
This is the Workroom, where curators check their notes before they build an exhibit. Answer one question at a time. If you miss one, read why, and keep going. That's how curators learn.

Visitors are lining up with questions! Read each question, then tap the case that answers it. And use each people's real name. The Haudenosaunee and the Maya are different nations, with their own languages and their own stories.
Last job of the day! Pick one culture case. Then write its label in three sentences. Say the people's real name, where they live or lived, and one thing they brought. When it's ready, open your case!
Read the visitor's question. Then tap the case that answers it.
Pick a case. Write three sentences in the box. Then open your case.
Drag the knob to the left, all the way to the start. Then come back to today.

Hoo, hello again, curator! Last time we filled the Natural Resources Shelf. Today our museum turns from the land to the people who live on it. This cart holds five things you might see any day. Each one came from a different people of our region. And remember our lens, courtesy. A good curator uses each people's real name, and gets the facts right.
Here is a simple map we made of our region. Show the five peoples one at a time, and see where each one lived. Then answer one question about the map.
This is the time rail. The right end is today. The left end is fifteen thousand years ago. Drag the knob to the left, and travel back in time. Watch who was living here.
Here's a word puzzle for you. The word root gen means born. It's hiding inside three words. Find it in each word, and then figure out what the word means.
Last job of the day! Pick one city. Pick its two clue tokens. Then write its settlement story in three sentences. When it's ready, open your exhibit!
Pick a city. Pick two clue tokens. Write three sentences. Then open your exhibit.
Read the city card. Then tap the token that shows why it grew.
Tap a spot on the model, or drag the pin to it. Try all five spots.

Hoo, welcome back, curator! Imagine this. It's a thousand years ago, and you are leading twenty families. You need a good spot for a new town. What should the land give you? Open the token box, and find out one need at a time.
These pictures were made long ago. Move the magnifier over each one, and look closely at the land and the water around each town.
Here is the Settlement Map, with six red pins. Read about one city at a time, then put the right token on its pin. Watch out. Some cities have more than one reason!
This is a model of some land, with five spots marked. Put your town pin on a spot, and watch what happens to your town. Try every spot, even the dry one.
Here's a word puzzle. The word root port means carry. Find it in three words, and figure out what each word means.
Your last job in this gallery! Pick two places. Find one thing from each, one difference, and one thing that connects them. Then install your panel, and watch what happens.
Pick two places. Pick one thing from each, and one connection. Write four sentences. Then install your panel.
Read each specimen card. Then drag it to its panel, or tap the panel's name.
Read the card. Tap where it started on the map. Then send it traveling.

Hoo, curator, look how far you've come! Seven rooms, all finished. This is the last room in our gallery. Four panels wait on the wall, one for each part of our region. Let's unveil them, and fill them with real specimens.
This map shows the language most people speak in each place. Turn on the colors one at a time. Then zoom in on the islands. Count how many colors you see!
Here's a curator secret. Cultures don't stop at borders. A sport or a song can start in one place, and travel to another. Follow each thread, and watch where it goes.
Word puzzle time! The word root lingu means tongue, or language. Find it in three words, and figure out what each word means.

Every gallery needs a directory sign by the door, so visitors know what is inside. First, finish the sentence that tells what a region is. Then pick one region, and tell visitors what makes it special. Then open the gallery!
Finish the sentence one blank at a time. Then pick a region and write a sentence of your own. Then open the gallery.
Look at the photo and read the card. Find the state on the small map. Then tap the alcove where it belongs.
Tap Lay down the sheet. Look at what it shows. Then answer the question. Do this for all four sheets.

This is the Light Table. Geographers lay see-through sheets over a map, one at a time. Each sheet shows one thing: the land, the weather, the resources, or how people live. Watch where the patterns line up. That is how regions are made!

Hoo, welcome to a brand-new gallery, the United States Regions Gallery! You have a new job, too. You are a United States Region Curator. The floor here is a giant map of our country. Find the state where you live, and tap it. Let's see which region it belongs to.
This is a real picture from space, taken at night. Every dot of light is a town or a city. Where are the lights crowded together? Where is it dark? The lights show where people chose to live.
Word puzzle time! The word root geo means earth. Find it in three words, and figure out what each word means.
Time to fill the Northeast alcove! Pick one object to put in front. Then write a label that tells visitors what makes the Northeast special. Then install it, and watch the alcove light up.
These two real photos show the same harbor in New York City, about one hundred years apart. Look at both. What changed? What stayed the same?
Pick one object to put in front. Write one sentence of your own in the box. Then install the alcove.
Lift out one object. Read its tag. Then tap the state it comes from on the map.
Turn the wheel to see all four seasons. Then answer the questions.
Hoo, curator! The first alcove is open: the Northeast. A crate just arrived, labeled Atlantic Coast. Let's lift out each object, one at a time. Read its tag, and find where it comes from on the map.
This window looks out on one hillside in Vermont. Turn the brass wheel to change the season. Watch the maple trees. They will show you how the Northeast changes all year long.
Word puzzle time! The word root mar means sea. Find it in three words, and figure out what each word means.
Time for twin labels! Pick one way the Northeast and the Southeast are alike, and one way they are different. Write both labels in your own words, and hang them between the two alcoves.
We're standing on a boardwalk in the Everglades. Look closely at the water and the plants. This wetland is full of life.
Tap a month to warm the ocean. Then start the storm and watch where it goes.
Pick one way they are alike and one way they are different. Write both labels in the box. Then hang them.
Drag the thermometer into each window, or tap the window. Then open the crate.
Hoo, curator! The second alcove is open: the Southeast. Look at these two windows. It's the same January day in Boston and in Miami. Check the thermometer in each one. Then open the new crate.
This is a storm tracker. First, warm up the ocean, month by month. Then watch what a hurricane needs to grow, and where it goes.
Word puzzle time! The word root therm means heat. Find it in three words, and figure out what each word means.
Time to fill the Midwest alcove! Pick one thing to put in front. Then write a label that tells visitors why the Midwest is called the Heartland. Install it, and watch the Great Lakes glow.
Pick one thing to put in front. Write one sentence of your own in the box. Then install the alcove.
Tap a thing on the shelf, or drag it to the scanner. Find out which Midwest state it comes from.
Tap each glowing circle in the window. Then fly lower. Do this three times.
These five lake beds are empty. Fill them with water, one at a time. Watch them glow!
Hoo, curator! The third alcove is open: the Midwest. Look at this store shelf. Scan each thing, and find out which Midwest state it comes from.
Buckle up! We're flying over the Midwest. From way up high, it looks like a quilt. Tap the glowing circles, then fly lower to see what's really down there.
Word puzzle time! The word root aqua means water. Find it in three words, and figure out what each word means.
This is my favorite model in the whole museum! A river runs across flat land made of rock layers. Drag the knob, and watch what millions of years can do.
Last step for this alcove! Write a sign that tells visitors three things: where the Southwest is, what the land is like, and something about the people. Then install it, and watch the sunset.
Drag the knob to the right to run time forward. Then tap each rock layer.
Start the rain. Then tap the jar you think is from Phoenix. Then open the crate.
Pick one idea for each part. Write your sign in the box. Then install the alcove.
Hoo, curator! The fourth alcove is open: the Southwest. These three jars catch one whole year of rain. One of them is from Phoenix, Arizona. Can you figure out which one?
Two little houses sit in the desert. One has thin walls. One has thick walls. Let's see what happens inside each one, at noon and at midnight.
Word puzzle time! The word root sol means sun. Find it in three words, and figure out what each word means.
This is it, curator: the last alcove! Write the West sign. Then tell visitors one pattern all five regions share, and one big difference. Install it, and watch the whole gallery light up!
Write the West sign. Pick a pattern and a difference. Then install the last alcove.
Drag Alaska out of its box to where it really is. Then do the same with Hawaii.
Tap the button to blow the wind. Then raise the mountains, and blow the wind again.
Deep under Hawaii, there is a hot spot. The ocean floor slides over it, very, very slowly. Move the ocean floor, and watch new islands grow!
Hoo, curator! The last alcove is the West, the biggest region of all. Look at this map. Alaska and Hawaii are tucked into little boxes. Let's find out where they really are!
Wet air blows in from the Pacific Ocean. Watch what happens when it bumps into tall mountains. One side gets lots of rain. Can you guess what happens to the other side?
Word puzzle time! The root volcan comes from Vulcan, the Roman god of fire. Find it in three words, and figure out what each word means.
The Listening Station is almost ready! Write the sign that welcomes visitors. Then flip the switch, and put the whole gallery on the air!
Turn on the radio. Then slide the dial to find each station, and guess where the music comes from.
Write three sentences for the sign. Then flip the switch to go on the air.
Drag a tape into the player, or tap it. Read along, then tap the tape's home region on the map.
Hoo, curator! A Listening Station just rolled into the gallery. Turn on the old radio and slide the dial. Each station plays real music from long ago. Can you guess which region it comes from?
This newspaper is folded up tight. Open it, and find what a good news story always tells you: what happened, when, where, and who helped.
Five tapes, five regions! There's a song, a legend, a poem, the news, and a story from the Hopi people. Play a tape, read along, and find its home on the map.
Word puzzle time! The root phon means sound. Find it in three words you might hear at the Listening Station.
This is the very last sign in the gallery! Write it, add someone from your own region, and then cut the ribbon. The whole gallery opens today!
Tap a cloth to uncover an object. Read the clue, then pick the person who made it.
Write the sign and the plaque. Then cut the ribbon.
Drag a name plaque onto its object, or tap the plaque and then tap the frame.
In Sequoyah's writing, one symbol stands for one whole sound. Tap the symbols to write the word Cherokee, just three symbols long!
Hoo, curator! One wall is still empty. This cart holds six covered objects. Each one belongs to a person who helped shape our country. Lift the cloths, and guess who made each one!
Time to hang the wall! Drag each name plaque to its object. Then watch the gold thread show where that person lived. Some of them moved to new places!
Word puzzle time! The root graph means to write. Find it in three words, and figure out what each word means.
This picture was taken from space, high above Kansas. Look at all those green circles! The Great Plains are dry here. So where does all that water come from?
The council meets next time. Write your evidence summary, put it in the folder, and press the seal. Then the council will be ready!
Drag each card to its region's tray. Or tap a card, then tap the tray.
Drag each chip to HAS or to GETS FROM OTHERS. Or tap the chip, then tap the column.
Pick one resource for each region. Write two sentences. Then press the seal.
This is the council ledger. Each region gets one page. Sort what the region has plenty of, and what it gets from other regions. Look for a pattern!
Hoo, Council Curator! Welcome to the Regional Council Chamber. Oh no, the evidence cards spilled all over the table! Put each card in the tray for its region.
Word puzzle time! The root vid, or vis, means to see. Find it in three words. Evidence is something you can see and check.
Now write your recommendation for the council. Pick a region, pick your evidence, and explain. Then the council will vote!
Press Melt the snow. Then tap each numbered water gate to take its share.
Press the wax seal to open the envelope. Then tap each seat to read its water report.
Drag each card to the side it helps, or tap a card, then tap a side. Then vote and give one reason.
Hoo, Council Curator! The council is in session. Break the seal on the envelope to read the council's question. Then check each region's water report.
The Colorado River starts as snow high in the Rocky Mountains. Seven states and Mexico all share it. Let's see what happens when everyone takes a turn!
An honest council looks at both sides. Put each evidence card on the side it helps. Then cast your vote and tell the council why.
Word puzzle time! The root re means again. Rain and snow refill rivers and lakes again, but only so fast. Find re in three words.
Now write the very first panel for the Marketplace Hall. Visitors will read it at the door. When it's ready, we open the hall!
Tap a loaf, then tap a family to give it to them. Or drag the loaf to a family.
Press Add the must-dos. Then tap the fun things you want to do today, until the day is full.
At each table, tap the thing you want most, or drag it into your basket.
Hoo, Trade and Choice Curator! Welcome to the Marketplace Hall. Three families are waiting at the bread booth, but look at the shelf. Hand out the bread and see what happens.
This is a real ration book from 1943. During World War Two, sugar, meat, and coffee were scarce. Every person got a book like this one. Let's look closely.
Your basket holds only three things. At each table, you can take one thing, not both. Watch the shadow shelf. It keeps what you gave up.
Word puzzle time! The word part un means not. When something is unlimited, it is not limited. Find un in three words.
Visitors want to know what happened at the trade tables. Write one sentence for each part of the panel. Then the two towns shake hands!
Tap the fish to load the coast cart and the grain to load the valley cart. Then send both carts down the road.
Read each card. Is it a trade or not a trade? Tap your answer.
Tap each HAS tag and each NEEDS tag to read it.
Hoo, Trade and Choice Curator! Two new tables came in overnight. One is from a coastal town, and one is from a valley farm. Read their tags. What does each town have, and what does it need?
This is a real place, the Hubbell Trading Post in Arizona. Navajo families brought wool and rugs here and left with flour, coffee, and sugar. Let's look closely.
This road joins the coast and the valley. Load each cart, send them down the road, and watch both pantries.
Word puzzle time! The word part ex means out. When you export something, you send it out to another place. Find ex in three words.

Curators, build four corners: Canada, the United States, Mexico and the Caribbean. Then send me one photo.
Before your headset, look at the models. Each one has a gray search word.
Put the globe in the middle. Then put one model in each alcove: Canada, the United States, Mexico and the Caribbean.
Open Library, then Camera. Fit your whole diorama in the tablet. Click Take photo, then send it on the Canvas tab.
Press the Meta button and click Quit. Then check that your photo is in the Canvas assignment.
Have more time? Make each model the same size. No corner is more important.
Curators, the Northeast has a rocky coast and busy harbors. Visit a lighthouse at night, then record a short video for me.
Before your headset, read about the place. Then press Practice and say your two sentences before the timer ends.
Open the On-Demand app. Click Explore. Type the map word, click the map, then click Begin Solo.
Move with the thumbstick. Look up at the light, then out at the water. Stand where you can see both.
Open Library, then Camera. Click Record video and say your two sentences. Click again to stop. Then send it on the Canvas tab.
Press the Meta button and click Quit. Then open the Canvas assignment and check that your video is there.
Have more time? Start your video on the water, then turn slowly up to the light.
